title: Sometimes it's hard
hookLine: some meditators have difficult experiences, and stopping or getting help is fine (Britton et al., 2017)

cards: Some people sit down to breathe, and something else comes up. Old memories they didn't ask for. A wave of fear.
A strange feeling that the world isn't quite real, or that they aren't. Most of what gets said about meditation is some version of: it's calming. And for many people, much of the time, it is.
So these people often tell no one, because everything they've read says this should feel peaceful, and they assume they're doing it wrong. A team of researchers decided to take them seriously.

teach.b: In 2017 a team at Brown University, led by Jared Lindahl with Willoughby Britton as senior researcher, published a study in the journal PLoS ONE called The varieties of contemplative experience.
They interviewed practitioners in Western Buddhist communities who had met difficulties in meditation, and teachers who had seen them in students.
They weren't counting how common these experiences are; they were mapping what they're like. The range was wide.

teach.h: FEAR, OLD MEMORIES, A CHANGED SELF.
teach.b: Fear, anxiety and panic. Old trauma resurfacing. Trouble sleeping.
Oversensitivity to light or sound. Changes in the sense of self. Some passed in days.
Some lasted much longer and affected people's work and relationships. Here's what makes this honest rather than frightening. Many contemplative traditions have known this for centuries.
Buddhist, Christian and Sufi teachers have long described hard passages in practice, one reason they insisted on teachers and community rather than sitting alone with a book.
The study's point wasn't that meditation is dangerous for everyone. It was that difficulties are real, they're not a sign you're failing, and people deserve to hear about them in advance.
So here is the plain guidance this path will always follow. If a practice feels wrong, you can stop. Open your eyes.
Feel your feet on the floor.

Move, walk, drink some water, talk to someone. Choose a gentler practice, or none for a while. If something lingers, talk to an experienced teacher, a doctor or a therapist, especially if you have a history of trauma.
And if you're ever in crisis, reach out to emergency help right away. Stopping is not failing.

how: Experienced meditation teachers watch for difficult experiences in students, suggest grounding and gentler practices, and refer people to clinicians when difficulties persist.

o: a doctor who proved meditation is unsafe for most people
a teacher who said true meditation always feels peaceful
a researcher who mapped hard experiences some meditators have

p: eyes open, feet on the floor

games.q: you're sitting and a wave of fear rises that won't settle. what does today's guidance say?
o: push through, it's part of the practice.
stop, ground yourself, and talk to someone.
games.why: stopping is always fine: open your eyes, feel your feet, move, and if it lingers, talk to a teacher or a clinician.

practice: This sit is about safety: keep your eyes softly open, feel your feet on the floor and your weight in the chair, and name three things you can see.
Breathe normally, knowing that at any moment you can stand up, stretch, or stop, and that would be exactly right. Just rest here, grounded.

wordCard.voice: Lindahl, lead author of the study mapping real difficulties some meditators meet, where stopping, grounding or getting help is always fine.

carryVoice: Your line: it's okay to stop. That holds for any practice, here or anywhere. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Lindahl, Fisher, Cooper, Rosen and Britton, 'The varieties of contemplative experience', PLoS ONE 12(5):e0176239 (2017)
